summary.text: For the ninth term, the primorial is \(P=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot17\cdot19\cdot23=223092870\), and \(P\equiv -41\pmod{29^2}\); since \((-41)^2+1=2\cdot29^2\), we have \(29^2\mid P^2+1\). Thus this term is not squarefree, disproving the conjunction regardless of the infinitude claim.

full_proof.text:
Let the primes be indexed from zero:
\[
p_0=2,\quad p_1=3,\quad p_2=5,\quad \ldots,
\]
and define the primorial
\[
P_n=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}p_k.
\]
Thus the sequence in question is
\[
a(n)=P_n^2+1.
\]
In particular, the empty product gives \(a(0)=2\), in agreement with the stated indexing.

We disprove the assertion that every \(a(n)\) is squarefree by considering \(n=9\). The first nine primes are
\[
2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23.
\]
Their product is
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_9
 &=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot17\cdot19\cdot23\\
 &=223{,}092{,}870.
\end{aligned}
\]
For example, the successive partial products are
\[
2,\ 6,\ 30,\ 210,\ 2310,\ 30030,\ 510510,\ 9{,}699{,}690,
\]
and multiplying the last of these by \(23\) gives \(223{,}092{,}870\).

Now consider the prime \(29\). It is indeed prime: since \(5^2<29<6^2\), any prime divisor of a composite number \(29\) would have to be at most \(5\), hence would be one of \(2,3,5\). But \(29\) is divisible by none of these: it is odd, it has remainder \(2\) modulo \(3\), and it has remainder \(4\) modulo \(5\).

We will show that \(29^2\) divides \(a(9)\). Since
\[
29^2=841,
\]
a direct division of the primorial gives
\[
223{,}092{,}870=841\cdot265{,}270+800.
\]
Consequently,
\[
P_9\equiv800\equiv-41\pmod{841}.
\]
Squaring and adding one therefore yields
\[
P_9^2+1\equiv(-41)^2+1=1681+1=1682=2\cdot841\equiv0\pmod{841}.
\]
It follows that
\[
29^2=841\mid P_9^2+1=a(9).
\]

For completeness, the term and the divisibility can also be displayed as an exact integer identity. Squaring the primorial and adding one gives
\[
a(9)=223{,}092{,}870^2+1
     =49{,}770{,}428{,}644{,}836{,}901,
\]
and
\[
49{,}770{,}428{,}644{,}836{,}901
 =841\cdot59{,}180{,}057{,}841{,}661.
\]
Thus the occurrence of \(29^2\) is an actual square divisor, not merely a divisibility suggested by reducing modulo \(29\).

A positive integer is squarefree precisely when no square of a prime divides it: in its prime factorization, squarefreeness means that every prime occurs with exponent at most one, while \(p^2\mid m\) means that the exponent of \(p\) is at least two. Here \(29\) is prime and \(29^2\mid a(9)\), so \(a(9)\) is not squarefree.

The proposed statement is the conjunction of
\[
\text{(i) every }a(n)\text{ is squarefree}
\]
and
\[
\text{(ii) }a(n)\text{ is prime for infinitely many }n.
\]
The counterexample \(n=9\) makes (i) false. Formally, if the conjunction were true, its first part would imply that \(a(9)\) is squarefree, contradicting the square divisor \(29^2\) found above. Hence the conjunction is false. No determination of whether infinitely many of the terms are prime is required for this disproof.
